title: Editorial Cartoons: Art as Satire
summary: Josh and Chuck explore editorial (political) cartoons: their decline at newspapers versus their continued life online and as memes, the satirical effect of caricature, and a history from Martin Luther and William Hogarth through James Gillray, Honore Daumier, Thomas Nast, Benjamin Franklin's "Join or Die" snake, World War II cartoonists Bill Mauldin and Dr. Seuss, Herb Block, and Charlie Hebdo. They close with the risks cartoonists face from editors and publishers, including Ann Telnaes quitting the Washington Post, and a listener email about a Scrabble score record.
topics: Uncle Sam and Santa Claus Nast

segments.title: Opening and decline of editorial cartoonists
segments.summary: Hosts introduce editorial cartoons (also called political cartoons) and note that full-time staff cartoonists at major newspapers have dropped from over 2,000 a century ago to fewer than twenty, though many still work online or through syndicates.

segments.title: Topicality of cartoons and satire
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how political cartoons are tied to the moment and lose their force over time, and how satire aims to influence opinion. Josh cites a Pope quote about satire, and they compare cartoons to the way caricature hits the brain harder than photographs.

segments.title: Mad magazine and the purpose of cartoons
segments.summary: Chuck mentions Mad magazine's political cartoons. The hosts discuss that cartoons use humor or sadness but always aim to prove a point, unlike comic strips.

segments.title: Origins: Martin Luther and William Hogarth
segments.summary: Martin Luther's unflattering woodcut prints of the pope and clergy, such as The Birth and Origin of the Pope from 1545, are described as possibly the first political cartoons, made possible by the printing press. Hogarth, considered the grandfather of political cartoons, later used exaggerated social satire.
topics: Birth and Origin of the Pope

segments.title: Benjamin Franklin and James Gillray
segments.summary: Franklin ran the segmented 'Join or Die' rattlesnake image in his Pennsylvania newspaper, rallying colonies before the French and Indian War. James Gillray, called the father of political cartoons, lampooned King George III and drew Pitt and Napoleon carving up the world as a plum pudding. Napoleon reportedly said Gillray did more than all the armies of Europe to bring him down.

segments.title: French satire and Honore Daumier
segments.summary: Magazines dedicated to satire emerged in the early nineteenth century, with France a center of satire. Honore Daumier was fined and jailed for caricaturing King Louis Philippe, including the Gargantua cartoon. The king said a caricature amounts to an act of violence.

segments.title: Thomas Nast and Boss Tweed
segments.summary: Thomas Nast, a German immigrant who drew for Harper's Weekly, made pro-union Civil War cartoons, including Compromise with the South, and was praised by Lincoln. He popularized Uncle Sam, the elephant and donkey, and a modern Santa Claus, and is credited with helping take down the corrupt Boss Tweed, though newspaper reporting also played a role.

segments.title: Immigration and child labor cartoons
segments.summary: Nast drew both anti-immigration and anti-Irish-immigrant cartoons. A 1903 Judge cartoon showed immigrants as rats, and a Puck cartoon mocked hyphenated Americans voting. A 1912 cartoon, From the Cradle to the Mill, depicted child labor with a grim reaper figure.

segments.title: Wartime censorship and World War One cartoons
segments.summary: A cartoonist was targeted under the Espionage Act in 1917 over the cartoon Having Their Fling, which criticized those cheering entry into war.

segments.title: World War II cartoons: Dr. Seuss and Bill Mauldin
segments.summary: Dr. Seuss drew wartime political cartoons for PM newspaper, including some with racist caricatures of Tojo. Bill Mauldin drew front-line cartoons with GIs Willy and Joe, touching on soldiers, homecoming, and the arrival of young replacements.

segments.title: Nazi cartoon and Jay Jackson's blind leading the blind
segments.summary: Hosts discuss a 1944 Norwegian Nazi cartoon, Kulturterror, criticizing American hypocrisy, and Jay Jackson's Chicago Defender cartoon depicting America and Germany as blind leaders over race hate. Chuck notes the Pulitzer for editorial cartooning began in 1922 and Mauldin won for WWII work.

segments.title: Herb Block and modern cartoonists
segments.summary: Herb Block, three-time Pulitzer winner for cartooning and public-service Pulitzer for Watergate, drew over a hundred Watergate cartoons and coined 'McCarthyism.' The Herb Block Prize is named for him. Pedro X. Molina, a finalist in 2024, draws for Counterpoint, and his outlet-with-Biden-and-Trump cartoon is discussed.

segments.title: Charlie Hebdo
segments.summary: Charlie Hebdo, a satirical paper since 1960, published a 2011 cover with a cartoon of the prophet Muhammad, followed by a firebombing and a 2012 cartoon. In 2015 two gunmen killed twelve people at the office, and the Je suis Charlie movement followed. Polls ten years later showed some shift in opinion.

segments.title: Newspapers, editors and cartoonists fired
segments.summary: Newspapers face declining subscriptions, and editors are more likely to pull cartoons or fire cartoonists after complaints. Mike Lukovich at the AJC is cited as a working cartoonist. Ann Telnaes criticized the trend and quit the Washington Post after seventeen years when editors refused to publish one of her cartoons.

segments.title: Political cartoons as memes
segments.summary: Josh argues that political cartoons have transformed into internet memes, using the 'This is Fine' dog comic as an example.

segments.title: Listener mail: Scrabble records
segments.summary: A listener named Reverend Eric describes his father's handmade ruled table recording his parents' Scrabble games and scores, which he now inherited. The hosts also acknowledge a earlier Simpsons Quigibow mention.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener emails and give the show credit.
